summary.text: A mushroom is the fleshy, spore-bearing fruiting body of a fungus, typically produced above ground on soil or another food source.
Mushrooms grow from underground mycelium and can expand rapidly under favorable conditions.
The word is more a common label for visible fungal fruiting bodies than a precise taxonomic term, and about 14,000 species are described.

facts.label: Spore print colors
facts.value: White most common, almost never blue, green or red

facts.label: Starting size
facts.value: A pinhead under two millimetres across

facts.label: Spore name
facts.value: Basidiospores, made on the gills of most

items.prompt: A forager sets a cap gill-side down on paper overnight. What will she get, and what is it for?

options.label: A powdery print whose colour helps classify and identify the mushroom
A stain showing which toxins the mushroom holds
A mark showing the mushroom's age in days
A seed imprint she can plant

items.explain: The spore print left by the cap helps in classifying and identifying mushrooms.

items.prompt: A hiker calls a pale cap 'obviously a toadstool, so poison'. Why is that unreliable?

options.label: Toadstool is the exact scientific name for any mushroom with a ring on its stalk
Every mushroom that has gills under its cap is known to be safe to eat
The names were never precisely defined, and edible and poisonous fungi are not clearly separated
Toadstool is a strict label that applies only to mushrooms that have pores

items.explain: The terms mushroom and toadstool were never precisely defined, and the line between edible and poisonous fungi is not clear-cut.

items.prompt: A child pulls up a mushroom and sees a web of fine white threads beneath it. What is the best reading?

options.label: The threads are roots drawing sugar for the mushroom's seeds
The threads are the fungus's body; the mushroom is its spore-bearing fruit
The threads are a second mushroom just starting to grow
The threads are mold growing on the mushroom

items.explain: A mushroom is the fruiting body of a fungus and grows from the mycelium, the mass of threadlike hyphae that makes up the fungus.

items.prompt: A mushroom has a skirt-like ring around the middle of its stalk. How did the ring get there?

options.label: It grew out of the stalk after the cap opened, to help feed it
It is a fold of the cap that dropped down and stuck to the stalk
It is an old root that was left behind as the stalk rose up
It is what is left of a thin tissue layer that covered the gills until the cap opened

items.explain: A partial veil covers the gills, and when the cap expands it breaks, leaving remnants such as a ring, or annulus, around the stalk.

items.prompt: A cook buys a 'lobster mushroom' with a strange shape and a red colour like boiled shellfish. What is it?

options.label: A mushroom of its own kind that happens to be red
A mushroom dyed red by iron in the soil
A different mushroom's fruit body deformed by a parasitic fungus
A shellfish living inside a fungus

items.explain: The lobster mushroom is the fruit body of a Russula or Lactarius mushroom deformed by the parasitic fungus Hypomyces lactifluorum, giving it a lobster-like shape and colour.

items.prompt: A friend says only things with blade-like gills under the cap deserve the name 'mushroom'. Why is that too narrow?

options.label: The name is used loosely for many visible fungal fruiting bodies, with pores, spines or other forms
Gills are a recent feature, and older mushrooms have none
Only mushrooms with pores count, and gilled ones are toadstools
Names are fixed by spore colour, not by anything under the cap

items.explain: Some mushrooms have pores or spines instead of gills, and the term is a common one for macroscopic fungal fruiting bodies rather than one with precise taxonomic meaning.

paragraphs.heading: What a mushroom is
paragraphs.text: A mushroom is the fleshy part of a fungus that carries spores, called its fruiting body, and it usually rises above the ground on soil or another food source. It grows out of the mycelium, the mass of thread-like hyphae that make up the fungus, which lies underground. In good conditions a mushroom can swell quickly. The word is a common label for fungal fruiting bodies big enough to see, not a precise scientific category. About 14,000 kinds of mushroom have been described.

paragraphs.heading: Gills and spores
paragraphs.text: Most mushrooms belong to the basidiomycetes and have gills, the blade-like parts under the cap. The gills make microscopic spores, which help the fungus spread. These spores, called basidiospores, are shot off structures named basidia and then drop between the gills through still air. They fall from under the cap as a fine rain of powder.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a spore print
paragraphs.text: Cut the cap off most mushrooms and leave it gills down overnight, and the falling spores leave a powdery pattern that copies the shape of the gills. This pattern is called a spore print, and its color helps both to classify and to identify mushrooms. Prints are most often white, but can be brown, black, purple-brown, pink, yellow or creamy; blue, green and red almost never turn up. Beginners have sometimes mistaken damp water marks on the paper for a white print.

paragraphs.heading: Naming a mushroom
paragraphs.text: Amateur and professional mycologists alike weigh many clues: juices that appear when the mushroom breaks, how it reacts to bruising, smell, taste, shade, habitat, growth habit and season. Tasting and sniffing carry their own risks, because of poisons and allergens. A local field guide can often get you to the genus out in the field, but naming the species takes more effort. Molecular methods are spreading fast, yet most people still use the traditional approach together with a microscope.

paragraphs.heading: From pinhead to button
paragraphs.text: A mushroom begins as a tiny knot less than two millimeters across, called a primordium, which forms within the mycelium on or near the surface it grows on. The primordium swells into a rounded, egg-like mass of woven hyphae called a button. In some mushrooms a cottony layer, the universal veil, wraps around the button. As the mushroom expands, this veil tears and may leave a cup at the base of the stalk or warty patches on the cap. Many mushrooms have no universal veil, so they show neither.

paragraphs.heading: Rings and veils
paragraphs.text: The gills are often hidden behind a second sheet of tissue, the partial veil. When the cap opens out, this veil breaks, and its remains may form a ring around the stalk or hang as scraps from the cap's edge. In some Amanita species the ring looks like a skirt, while in many Lepiota species it looks more like a collar. In Cortinarius only faint traces remain of a cobweb-like veil called a cortina.

paragraphs.heading: Mushrooms off the usual pattern
paragraphs.text: The lobster mushroom is a Russula or Lactarius mushroom that a parasitic fungus has twisted out of shape. The result is oddly formed and red, much like a boiled lobster. Other fungi called mushrooms have no gills: some have pores underneath, and others, such as the hedgehog mushroom, have spines. Puffballs, stinkhorns, cup fungi, bracket fungi, coral fungi and jelly fungi have all been called mushrooms too.
